young.html: The Republic is Plato's most famous book. It begins with a simple question at a friend's house: What is justice? In other words, what does it mean to be fair and good to others, and is it worth it?

Plato's brother Glaucon tells a story to make the question hard. A shepherd named Gyges finds a magic ring. When he turns it on his finger, he becomes invisible! Nobody can see what he does, so nobody can punish him. Gyges uses the ring to do terrible things and make himself king. Glaucon asks: if you had that ring, would you still be good? If people are only good because they might get caught, is goodness really worth anything?

To find the answer, Socrates imagines building a whole city from scratch, in words. A good city, he says, has three groups who each do their own job well: rulers who are wise, soldiers who are brave, and workers who grow food and make things. Then he says each person has the same three parts inside: a thinking part, a brave part and a wanting part. You are just, he says, when your thinking part is in charge and all three work together.

young.name: gb-city-soul
young.cap: Tap a row: the part of the city, the matching part of the soul, and its virtue. Then try “Unjust.”

young.html: The ring of Gyges. Each person in the family writes down, privately, one thing they would do if they were invisible for a day. Read them aloud (no names). Which ones would be fine even if everyone could see? Which ones would not? What does that tell you about why we are good?

full.html: The Republic (about 375 BC) has ten books, which are really chapters. Socrates narrates it himself. He has gone down to Athens' port, the Piraeus, for a festival, and a group of friends persuades him to stay at the house of Cephalus, a rich old man. Plato's own brothers, Glaucon and Adeimantus, are among the speakers. This rung covers Books I–V; the next covers VI–X.

full.cap: The three answers of Book I, in our own words.

full.html: Thrasymachus, a sophist, bursts in angrily:

full.text: Listen, then, he said; I proclaim that justice is nothing else than the interest of the stronger. And now why do you not praise me? But of course you won't.
full.author: Plato
full.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. III, Clarendon Press

full.html: Socrates argues him into silence, but at the end of Book I admits that they have argued about whether justice pays before saying what it is.

Glaucon wants a real answer. Most people, he says, think justice is a deal: we agree not to harm each other because we fear being harmed. To show this, he tells of the shepherd Gyges, who found a gold ring:

full.text: …as he was sitting among them he chanced to turn the collet of the ring inside his hand, when instantly he became invisible to the rest of the company and they began to speak of him as if he were no longer present. He was astonished at this, and again touching the ring he turned the collet outwards and reappeared…
full.author: Plato
full.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. III, Clarendon Press
full.note: The collet is the setting of the ring's stone.

full.html: Gyges uses the ring to seize the throne. Glaucon says anyone would do the same if they could never be caught. He challenges Socrates to show that justice is good in itself, even for someone with a bad reputation, not just for its rewards.

full.text: Books II–IV: the city in words

full.html: Socrates suggests looking for justice in something larger first, a city, where it may be easier to see. A simple city of farmers and craftspeople grows into a richer one that needs soldiers. From them Socrates picks out guardians, carefully educated in music, poetry and physical training. He wants to keep stories that show gods behaving badly away from the young, and he proposes a founding myth, sometimes called the “noble lie,” that people are born with gold, silver or bronze in their souls, fitting them to rule, guard or work.

full.name: gb-city-soul
full.cap: The three classes and three parts. Choose “Unjust” to see the order reversed.

full.html: The four virtues. The city is wise because its rulers are wise, brave because its soldiers are, moderate because all classes agree about who should rule, and just because each class does its own work and does not meddle in the others'. In the soul, reason should rule, with spirit as its ally, over appetite. Justice is the healthy order of the soul; injustice is like a sickness.

Socrates' friends make him explain three startling proposals, which he calls waves that might drown him in laughter. First, women with the right gifts should be guardians, with the same education as men. Second, the guardians should have no private families or property, sharing all things. Third, the boldest:

full.text: Until philosophers are kings, or the kings and princes of this world have the spirit and power of philosophy, and political greatness and wisdom meet in one, and those commoner natures who pursue either to the exclusion of the other are compelled to stand aside, cities will never have rest from their evils…
full.author: Plato
full.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. III, Clarendon Press

full.html: Thinking the Republic is mainly a plan Plato wanted put into practice. Near the end, Socrates says there is “laid up a pattern of it” in heaven, for anyone who wants to set his own soul in order, whether or not such a city ever exists. Readers disagree about how literally Plato meant the city. The next rung explains why a philosopher should rule.

Aristotle, in the second book of his Politics (on this ladder), objected that a city made too unified stops being a city, and that what belongs to everyone is cared for by no one. Some modern readers, such as Karl Popper, saw the Republic's rule by an unelected few and its control of stories as dangerous. Others defend Plato as asking a fair question: who should be trusted with power, and how should they be educated? The proposal that women could be rulers was very unusual in his time.

full.title: Is justice worth it?
full.q: Lay out Glaucon's challenge as an argument, and say what Socrates must show.
steps: Glaucon's premise: people are just only because they fear the penalties of being unjust.
Then: someone who could never be caught (the ring) would have no reason to be just.
So, Glaucon says, justice is not good in itself, only for its rewards.
To answer, Socrates must show that justice is good for the soul in itself, whatever its reputation. He argues that it is the soul's health and right order.
full.a: Socrates must show that being just is better than being unjust, even with no reward

deep.html: The Republic's central idea is an analogy: the city is the soul “writ large.” Many readers think the main subject is the soul, and the city is a magnifying glass. Others think Plato meant both. The same three-part soul appears in the Phaedrus's chariot (reason, spirit, appetite). Later writers from Aristotle to Freud, much later on this ladder, offered their own divisions of the mind.

Glaucon's account, that justice is an agreement made out of fear, is an early form of social contract theory. Thomas Hobbes, later on this ladder, took up a version of it and turned it into an argument for strong government. Plato's Socrates rejects it: justice, he says, is not a bargain but the health of the soul.

items: Would you be good if no one could ever find out? What does your answer show?
Is justice the same thing in a person and in a country?
Who should be in charge of a group: the wisest, the most popular, or everyone together? What are the risks of each?

questions: If you found the ring of Gyges, what would you do with it? Be honest!
Cephalus says justice is telling the truth and paying back what you owe. Can you think of a time when that would not be the fair thing to do?
Do you have a thinking part, a brave part and a wanting part? When do they disagree?
Socrates thought rulers should be the wisest people. What makes a good leader?
Aristotle said that what belongs to everyone is cared for by no one. Is that true at home or at school?
Why does Glaucon want to know whether justice is good in itself, and not just because of its rewards?
care: The Republic discusses government, war and the ideal city. The lesson presents Plato's proposals and their critics fairly, without taking sides on modern political questions.
